identity.title: Food Safety Plan (FSMA Preventive Controls for Human Food): ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips, Salem Plant
identity.issuer: Willamette Valley Foods, Inc. (prepared by Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager / PCQI)
identity.site: Salem — 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301

scan.summary: This is the plant's own written food safety plan under FDA's Preventive Controls for Human Food rule (21 CFR Part 117, Subpart C). It is the company's document, so it can be fixed, and FDA or Oregon Department of Agriculture inspectors will judge the plant against it. The core parts are there: a hazard analysis, preventive controls, monitoring, corrective actions, verification, supply-chain, records and training sections. But the recall plan is missing, and the plan does not deal with Salmonella in tahini and other ingredients that are added after the cook step. The supply-chain program, validation, owner sign-off and the procedures for a few controls are also thin or absent.
scan.freshness_note: The plan took effect on May 12, 2025, so it is about 16 months old. It has to be reanalyzed at least every 3 years (by about May 12, 2028), and sooner if a product, ingredient, supplier or process changes, or if new hazard information comes up. Check whether a newer revision exists and whether anything has changed since May 2025.

gaps.title: No written recall plan
gaps.description: The plan names several hazards that need a preventive control (sesame, Listeria, Salmonella, metal). When that is true, the food safety plan has to include a written recall plan: how to notify customers and the public, how to check the recall worked, and how to handle the recalled product. There is no recall section anywhere.
gaps.fix: Add a recall plan section. It should cover who decides on a recall, how direct customers in Oregon, Washington and Idaho are told, when to notify FDA and the public, effectiveness checks, and whether recalled product is reworked, reconditioned or destroyed. Tie it to the lot and date codes already applied at the date coding step.

gaps.title: Salmonella in tahini and other ingredients added after the cook is not addressed
gaps.description: The hazard analysis treats the bean cook as the kill step for the finished product. But the process flow shows tahini, lemon juice, garlic and spices are blended in after cooking and cooling, so the cook does nothing to pathogens in those ingredients. Tahini has been linked to Salmonella outbreaks and recalls, and spices and garlic can carry pathogens too. For tahini, the only hazard listed is the sesame allergen.
gaps.fix: Revise the hazard analysis for every ingredient added after the cook, including Salmonella in tahini and spices. Decide on a control for each: for example, a supply-chain-applied control with supplier verification, or buying treated or pasteurized ingredients with documented verification. Then add that control to Section 4.
gaps.quote: Cook step is the kill step for the finished product

gaps.title: Supply-chain program is missing required elements
gaps.description: Section 8 says only that suppliers are approved, send an audit certificate and send a certificate of analysis for each lot. Part 117 Subpart G requires more in writing: which hazards the supplier controls, who approves suppliers, how verification activities and their frequency are chosen, and how records are reviewed. If the supplier controls a hazard that can cause serious illness or death (likely Salmonella in tahini), the default verification is an annual onsite audit, and the company reviews the audit results. Holding a certificate is not the same thing.
gaps.fix: Expand Section 8. For each raw material, name the hazard the supplier controls. Record the supplier approval procedure. Choose and document verification activities (an onsite audit for Salmonella in tahini unless another activity is justified in writing). Say how certificates of analysis and audit reports are reviewed. List the records kept.
gaps.quote: Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate

gaps.title: Stones in dry beans have no working control
gaps.description: The hazard analysis says stones and metal in dry beans are controlled at metal detection and by supplier screening. A metal detector does not find stones. Section 4 has no control for stones and no written supplier control for them either.
gaps.fix: Add a control for stones and other non-metal foreign material, such as bean sorting or destoning, visual inspection at receiving or soaking, or a documented supplier-applied control with verification. Add the monitoring and corrective action to go with it.
gaps.quote: Field debris in dry beans, controlled at metal detection and by supplier screening

gaps.title: Cold storage is listed as needing a control, but there is no control, monitoring or corrective action
gaps.description: Section 3 says Listeria growth during refrigerated storage requires a preventive control. Section 4 has no refrigeration control, Section 5 does not monitor storage temperature, and Section 6 has no corrective action for a temperature problem. The 41°F holding temperature only appears in the product description.
gaps.fix: Add a refrigeration control with the 41°F limit, continuous or scheduled temperature monitoring of cold storage, a corrective action for temperature deviations (hold and evaluate the product), and review of the temperature records.
gaps.quote: Refrigerated RTE product with a 45-day shelf life

gaps.title: Hazard analysis leaves out chemical hazards and some biological ones
gaps.description: The hazard analysis has no chemical hazards at all. The rule requires considering chemical hazards such as pesticide residues, natural toxins, sanitizer residues and unapproved additives. It also does not look at Clostridium botulinum or product pH/acidity in a refrigerated, sealed ready-to-eat product with a 45-day shelf life, or at other allergens that may be in the plant.
gaps.fix: Have the PCQI redo the hazard analysis to cover chemical hazards, including radiological ones, for every ingredient and step. Document the reasoning on C. botulinum and pH/shelf life, and confirm whether any allergens besides sesame are present.

gaps.title: No validation of the cook and cooling limits
gaps.description: Process controls have to be validated by or under a PCQI, showing the limits actually control the hazard. The plan does not mention validation for the cook or the cooling step. The cook limit is also an internal temperature of 212°F. That is the boiling point at sea level, and an open kettle in Salem may not reliably reach it (this is my inference, and I am not certain of it). If so, the plan would call for re-cooks that never end, or its own limit would be quietly ignored.
gaps.fix: Document validation for the cook and cooling steps (scientific literature, a process authority, or in-plant studies). Set a cook limit the kettle can actually meet at this elevation and that is supported by the validation.
gaps.quote: Minimum 212°F for 60 minutes, measured with a calibrated probe thermometer

gaps.title: Environmental monitoring and product testing procedures are incomplete
gaps.description: Written procedures for environmental monitoring and product testing have to name the test organism, sampling locations, number of samples, timing, test method, the laboratory, and the corrective action. The plan gives 10 sites a week in zones 1 and 2 and monthly finished-product testing. It does not name the sampling sites, the laboratory, the test methods, how many product samples are taken, or what happens to product if the finished-product test is positive.
gaps.fix: Add or attach a written environmental monitoring procedure (site map, rotation, zone 3 and 4 sites, the lab, the method) and a product testing procedure (samples per lot, lot hold until results, the lab, the method, and the corrective action for a positive result).
gaps.quote: Finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory.

gaps.title: Label check at packaging is not monitored
gaps.description: The allergen control calls for a label review at receipt and at printing. The monitoring section only covers the label check at receipt. Nothing records a check that the right label is on the right product on the line, for example that a sesame label is on the hummus when a changeover happens.
gaps.fix: Add monitoring at filling and labeling: a label check at start-up, at each product changeover and periodically, recorded on a log, with a corrective action for any product labeled wrong.
gaps.quote: The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs the label log.

gaps.title: Plan is not signed and dated by the owner, operator or agent in charge
gaps.description: The approval line gives a job title but no name, signature or date. The food safety plan has to be signed and dated by the owner, operator or agent in charge when it is first completed and each time it is changed.
gaps.fix: Have the plant manager or owner sign and date the plan with a printed name. Add a revision history table.

gaps.title: No reanalysis schedule or triggers
gaps.description: The plan does not say it will be reanalyzed at least every 3 years, or when a change in activities, new hazard information, an unexpected problem or an ineffective control calls for reanalysis.
gaps.fix: Add a reanalysis section: at least every 3 years (next by May 12, 2028) and whenever one of the triggers in 117.170 happens, carried out or overseen by the PCQI.

scan.confidence_notes: All seven pages are clear, typed text. I read the title, site, effective date and preparer from the cover (page 1). I am confident about the missing recall plan, the unsigned approval line, the cold-storage control that is listed but never built out, the absent reanalysis section, and the thin supply-chain section. These come from well-established Part 117 requirements, which I cited from memory and did not re-check online. The Salmonella-in-tahini finding, the stones finding and the missing chemical and C. botulinum review are my own inferences from the process flow and the hazard table. They are strong, but a PCQI's written reasoning could answer some of them. The 212°F cook-limit concern depends on the plant's elevation and equipment, and my confidence in it is low. I did not judge the science behind the specific limits (the cooling times, the metal detector test-piece sizes). The schema has no field for page references, so they are given in the locators and here.

WILLAMETTE VALLEY FOODS, INC.
FOOD SAFETY PLAN
Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips
Salem Plant, 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301
Effective date: May 12, 2025
Prepared by: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager, Preventive Controls Qualified Individual
(PCQI certificate, FSPCA course, March 2024)
Approved by: Plant Manager
1. Facility and product description
Willamette Valley Foods produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-ounce and 16-
ounce sealed plastic tubs for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. The Salem plant operates one
shift, five days a week, with 28 production employees. Products are made from cooked chickpeas or black
beans, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt and spices, blended, filled, sealed, coded and held
refrigerated at or below 41°F. Shelf life is 45 days refrigerated. Products are labeled with the allergen
statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
2. Process flow
Receiving of dry beans, tahini and other ingredients → dry storage or refrigerated storage → soaking and
cooking of beans (kettle, 212°F, 60 minutes minimum) → cooling in the blast chiller → blending with
other ingredients → filling and sealing → date coding → metal detection → refrigerated storage →
shipping.

beans (Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes) product

4. Preventive controls

Vegetative Cook beans in the kettle to an internal temperature of at Process Minimum 212°F for 60 minutes, measured
pathogens at cook least 212°F for at least 60 minutes with a calibrated probe thermometer
Spore-former Cool cooked beans from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours Process 135°F to 70°F in 2 hours; 70°F to 41°F in
growth at cooling and to 41°F within a further 4 hours in the blast chiller 4 hours
Listeria in the Sanitation of food-contact surfaces before each Sanitation ATP swab pass before start-up; Listeria
RTE environment production run and between products; environmental spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2
monitoring swabs weekly
Sesame allergen Allergen labeling review for every label at receipt and at Allergen Label matches the formulation sheet;
printing; product scheduling with hummus items last in washdown verified by ATP swab before
the day, followed by full washdown the next non-sesame product
Metal Metal detection of every sealed tub Process Reject at 2.0 mm ferrous, 2.5 mm non-
ferrous, 3.0 mm stainless test pieces
5. Monitoring
The kettle operator records the internal temperature and the time at the start and end of each cook batch
on the cook log. The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling
log. The sanitation lead records the ATP swab result before each start-up. The line lead runs the three
metal test pieces through the detector at start-up, every two hours, and at the end of the run, and records
the result. The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs
the label log.
6. Corrective actions
If a cook batch does not reach 212°F for 60 minutes, the batch is re-cooked to the critical limit or
discarded, and the cause is recorded. If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded. If an ATP
swab fails, the surface is re-cleaned and re-swabbed before production starts. If a Listeria spp. swab is
positive, the site is cleaned and re-swabbed, adjacent sites are added, and product made on that line since
the last negative swab is held pending investigation. If the metal detector fails a test piece, all product
since the last passing test is re-run through the detector. If a label does not match the formulation, the lot
is quarantined and not used. All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed
by the PCQI within seven days.
7. Verification
The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven
working days of their creation. Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly,
and the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually. Finished product is tested for Listeria
monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory. Environmental monitoring results are trended
quarterly.
8. Supply-chain program
Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit
certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The approved supplier list is maintained by the quality
manager.
9. Records
All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record
and are available to FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture on request. Records are reviewed and
signed by the PCQI as described in section 7.
10. Training
All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually. The PCQI holds a current
FSPCA certificate. Sanitation and line leads are trained on the monitoring procedures in this plan.
